savings_residuals.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved Code of Fair Competition of the Paper and Pulp Industry before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences that the repeal did not turn into continuing commands; nothing in S.J. Res. 113 (SUPPLEMENT:SJRES113) continues the approval after June 14, 1935. Any antitrust exemption for complying action before the repeal (NIRA section 5, SUPPLEMENT:NIRA5) is likewise an accrued effect; the resolution's proviso, which extends the exemption only to "agreements and action thereunder" meeting stated conditions, leaves open how far it narrowed the exemption for past action, so the claim records no continuing exemption and no surviving approval. The 1944 WPA numbered list (jobs/x1-class-engine/data/WPA_NUMBERED_ENTRIES.csv) carries the same number and date: 'Code of Fair Competition for the Medium and Low Priced Jewelry Manufacturing Industry approved. IV NRA Codes 355. (Dec 23, 1933)'. Quotations are taken from the registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy. EO 6530 (December 23, 1933) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Medium and Low Priced Jewelry Manufacturing Industry 'subject to the following condition: That the application of the provision of sub-section (b), Section 1, Article III, which provides for the payment of time and one third for all hours worked by any employee in excess of forty (40) per week, shall be stayed until March 1, 1934, at which time such provision shall become effective and have the same force and effect as any other provision of the Code.' The dossier's single clause (characters 757-1620) holds two commands with different lifetimes, so the inventory is corrected on the registered text into two scopes: the approval sentence (757-1158) and the stay condition (1160-1525); the signature block and Administrator's recommendation that follow are not operative. Stay condition: it ends by its own terms on 1934-03-01, recorded inclusive (the stay runs through that day) under the owner's 2026-10-21 ruling; the words 'at which time such provision shall become effective' support the exclusive reading, under which the stay stops when March 1, 1934 begins and the overtime provision applies that day. Approval: First end: 1935-06-14, the day Senate Joint Resolution 113 (Public Resolution No. 26, 74th Congress, 49 Stat. 375, chapter 246) was approved. Section 2 of the resolution reads: 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed', with one proviso that narrows only the section 5 antitrust exemption. It names no code and no order, so it is not a naming instrument (owner ruling 2026-10-21, unnamed instruments), and under the owner's 2026-10-28 ruling a general rule ends a command only where something shows it extinguished that command. What shows it here is the text of the Act under which the order was made (48 Stat. 195, held): section 3(a) is the power to approve a code; section 3(b) makes the provisions of an approved code 'the standards of fair competition for such trade or industry' and a violation an unfair method of competition; section 3(c) gives the district courts jurisdiction to restrain violations of 'any code of fair competition approved under this title'; and section 10(b) lets the President cancel or modify 'any order, approval, license, rule, or regulation issued under this title', which shows the approval was a continuing act that the Act made binding through sections 3(b) and 3(c). The approval commands nothing of its own beyond that statutory operation, and the resolution repealed the approval power and the enforcement of codes together, with no clause preserving approved codes. The order's only operative act, making the code the enforceable standard, therefore ended on 1935-06-14. Alternatives considered and disclosed. (a) Earlier: Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935 (caption and syllabus held), says at 542 'the code-making authority thus conferred is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power'. The judgment concerned the Live Poultry Code; it names no other code, and nothing held shows it extinguished this approval on that date (no order of May 27 through June 14 touches any code). If a reviewer holds it ended every approval, the first end would be 1935-05-27; the claim uses June 14 because that is the first date on which held text removes approval and enforcement for all codes. (b) The original expiry of Title I two years after enactment (section 2(c), June 16, 1935) was displaced when the resolution amended section 2(c) to April 1, 1936; it is later than the repeal. (c) Later: EO 7076 (June 15, 1935, held APP text, page record date 1935-06-15; its held transcription omits the signature and date lines) amends all existing Title I executive orders 'so as to continue them in effect and to extend their operation ... until April 1, 1936, so far as consistent with the provisions of the National Industrial Recovery Act as amended and extended', but provides that it 'shall not be construed as an exercise by the President of any authority, or as authorizing any person or agency ... to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition, to provide for the enforcement of such codes'. Because the approval's force came through the provisions the resolution had repealed the day before, continuing it 'so far as consistent' with the Act as amended leaves it no enforceable operation; EO 7076 is therefore recorded here as a disclosed later order and is not treated as an extension or an end. Held EO 7075 (June 15, 1935) likewise refers to the trades 'heretofore subject to codes of fair competition'. (d) A reviewer who reads section 5 as keeping approved codes 'in effect' for antitrust exemption while Title I stood (to April 1, 1936, plus sixty days) could place a later end for that statutory exemption; the exemption is a statutory consequence, not a command of this order, and the resolution's proviso narrowed it to agreements on section 7(a) requirements and on practices already unlawful. That reading would not revive the approval as an enforceable code. Limit: the approved code's own text is not held, so a duration or cancellation term inside it could not be read; no held order, statute, case or index entry shows a code-specific cancellation, amendment, supersession or expiry. Searches run 2026-10-29. (1) A scan of 51,237 txt, jsonl, csv, json and md files under jobs/ (skipping the derivative folders clause-drafts, claim-kit, case-bundles, claim-drafts, x1-class-engine, readiness-tracker and domesday-register, and cache, capture and pdf folders) for the code's title and for citations of this order by number. (2) Every held order text numbered 7060 or higher (APP, Hathi/Commons printed copies, Wikisource, Federal Register, source-ladder) containing the phrase 'codes of fair competition': only EO 7075, EO 7076 and EO 7323 (and an unrelated 1941 board order, EO 9027). (3) The APP index of orders dated 1935-05-15 through 1935-06-25: no order dated 1935-05-27 through 1935-06-14 touches an NRA code; EO 7075 and 7076 (June 15) and EO 7084 and 7085 (June 24, labor boards) are the next NRA orders. (4) The later-events counter-evidence leads file (none for this order). (5) The machine searches current-law:usc and current-law:ecfr (0 hits) and later-events:ofr_catalog (0 hits; its coverage starts in 1937, so it is not relied on alone). Result of (1): hits are only this order's own records and index rows. The phrase 'time and one third' also appears in EO 6393 (Toy and Playthings code) and EO 6450 (Precious Jewelry Producing code), which are other codes and do not mention this order or its stay.

savings_residuals.reason: The order states no savings. What survives the repeal is statutory and accrued, not a continuing command of the approval: liabilities and rights that accrued while the code was binding (violations before 1935-06-14, and conduct that complied with it), and the section 5 antitrust exemption for action complying with an approved code 'while this title is in effect ... and for sixty days thereafter' (held, 48 Stat. 195), as narrowed by the resolution's proviso. versions.research_rationale:
The complete official original was compared with its target page: EO 8179 has three numbered amendments, including all nested conditions; EO 8300 has one amendment of the first sentence of Rule VII section 2(b). The originals contain no sunset, completed assignment, or independent command outside those host-rule amendments. Probation and objection conditions govern recurring application rather than ending the entire order. EO 8707 and EO 8423 are later amendments, with before-and-after text retained. The earlier ACT commentary that EO 8707 ended EO 8179 item 2 is reconsidered under the owner's October 21 strike-and-insert ruling, which continues the amended clause.

The full text and operative pages of EO 9830 were examined. Its opening May 1, 1947 effective date governs Parts I, II and III. Part II replaces the Civil Service Rules, and Part III expressly names both target orders and their original dates without a savings qualification. Every original footprint therefore ends on May 1, 1947 under the owner's October 21 unnamed-instruments convention. This is the convention's named endpoint, not a claim that no substantive application changed earlier. The earlier War Service Regulations and 1946 temporary regulations are pinned and expressly disclosed as candidate earlier changes. The 1942 list does not include Rule XI. The 1946 effective-date qualification is preserved rather than converted to an unsupported exact date.

EO 9691 and temporary regulation 27.16(g) protect acquired rights, tenure and benefits. These are separately analyzed as saved acts and successor authority, not silently erased or treated as current authority under the revoked target orders. No independent target command or present application of the old target terms was identified in the bounded later-source, host-rule, savings and revival checks. The U.S. Code machine search reaches October 9 only; it is not the sole bridge to the October 14, 2026 cutoff. This is a producer proposal under the existing codebook and owner rulings, subject to independent whole-case review and human review of the disclosed earlier candidates.

Correction after independent review: EO8514 is a distinct earlier exception affecting item2. It permits Commission-approved probationary transfers into positions directly concerned with national defense without a six-month minimum. EO8707 does not subsume it. The authorization begins on August13,1940 under its immediate operative wording and is expressly revoked by EO9691 section9 on February4,1946. The acquired-reemployment-rights saving is retained without assuming all rights were extinguished or all other wartime limitations were removed. versions.research_rationale:
EO 9301 (February 9, 1943, Franklin D. Roosevelt; 8 FR 1825, issue of Thursday, February 11, 1943), read in full in the held Federal Register text, declares that "For the duration of the war" no plant or place of employment is deemed to make the most effective use of manpower if its minimum workweek is under 48 hours (section 1, inside the lead row of the machine inventory), directs agencies to require contractors to comply (2), authorizes the Chairman of the War Manpower Commission to interpret the order and issue policies, directives and regulations and to set a different workweek in particular cases (3), requires agencies to comply (4) and states that the order is not to supersede other hours or wage laws (5). EO 9607 (August 30, 1945), held Federal Register text, revokes it by number in one sentence. The phrase "For the duration of the war" is an own-terms condition; no held instrument or source fixes a legal end of the war before August 30, 1945, and EO 9607 revokes the order outright without reciting that it had lapsed, so the first end is the express revocation.

EO 9521 (Feb. 13, 1945) revoked this order only 'as of the dates of issu­ance of the orders or regulations of the Secretary of State that cover the subject-matter of and supersede' it, and no held source identifies such a Secretary of State order or regulation, or its date, for the tariff item (para. 1) or the notarial regulations changed by paras. 2 and 3. Later tariff orders still treat the Tariff as 'amended by' EOs 9303 and 9407 (EO 9591, July 21, 1945; EO 9767, Aug. 9, 1946), and EO 10697 sec. 7 revoked this order only 'To the extent that they have not heretofore been revoked or superseded', effective March 1, 1957 (sec. 8). versions.research_rationale: EO 9303 (Feb. 11, 1943; 8 FR 1911) has three operative paragraphs amending the Foreign Service Regulations of EO 7968: para. 1 rewrites item 30 of the Tariff of Foreign Service Fees (no fee for notarial and other services to foreign officials who give reciprocal courtesies); para. 2 revokes secs. V-49 to V-52; para. 3 deletes 'in the handwriting of the officer' from sec. V-54(d). The 1989 Codification gives 'Revoked by EOs 9521, 10697'. EO 9521 revoked the listed orders only as of the issuance of Secretary of State regulations superseding them, and EO 9591 (1945) and EO 9767 (1946) still describe the Tariff as amended by this order, so EO 9521 had not operated on the tariff item by 1946; EO 10697 sec. 7 revoked whatever remained, effective March 1, 1957. Every clause is terminated by 1957 at the latest, but which date ends each paragraph depends on Secretary of State regulations not held, so first_end is left open. The para. 1 table is printed with the item number misread as '80' in the OCR. No human certification is asserted.

savings_residuals.reason: Neither EO 9521 nor EO 10697 preserves anything under this order (EO 9521's provisos concern the Secretary's designations and non-revival of earlier orders; EO 10697 has no savings clause and prescribes a complete new Tariff of Fees). The order's effects were fee exemptions and regulation text for consular services; services already rendered without fee are completed transactions, not continuing effects. Bounded search: this order, EO 9521, EO 9591, EO 9767 and EO 10697 in full.

versions.research_rationale: EO 9591 of July 21, 1945 (official text 10 FR 9205, saved OCR text layer of the govinfo issue PDF read in full). The OCR interleaves columns: the order's heading, enacting clause and paragraphs 1-2 run continuously, then text of EO 9592 and a Civil Service Commission rule intervene before the signature block 'July 21,1945' with F.R. Doc. 45-13508 (EO 9592 carries 45-13509 and its own signature), so the order consists of paragraphs 1 and 2 only. Paragraph 1's opening words are quoted up to the parenthetical citation because the OCR fuses footnote markers to the cited order numbers there (the fused figures are not valid order numbers); the parenthetical cites EO 7968 as amended by EOs 8297, 9303, 9407 and 9507. Paragraph 1 amends Tariff Items 6, 8 and 34; paragraph 2 amends section V-23 of the Foreign Service Regulations. EO 9767 (1946) and EO 10473 (1953) changed other sub-items of Item 6 but not the eighth heading 'Issue of card or certificate of identity and registration' (EO 10473 inserts a new item immediately below it, so it still stood in 1953), Item 8 or Item 34; EO 10639 (1955) deleted only Items 1-5. EO 10697 (22 FR 777, read in full) prescribed a complete new Tariff effective March 1, 1957 and in section 7 revoked EO 9591, so paragraph 1's clauses first ended 1957-03-01. Paragraph 2 is left open (see the gap): its host section V-23 may have lapsed earlier. This is a partial claim: original text, clause inventory, savings and later-source search are asserted; the ending is not.

savings_residuals.reason: EO 10697 contains no savings or transition clause. It prescribes a complete new Tariff of Fees and its own collection rules (sections 1-6), effective March 1, 1957, and revokes the earlier tariff orders to the extent not already revoked or superseded. Fees charged under the earlier tariff were completed transactions; the order created no fund, office, property or vested right that survived. Paragraph 2's wording change and revocation in section V-23 of the Foreign Service Regulations created no fund, office, property or vested right either.

Approved  Code  No.   119 CODE  OF  FAIR  COMPETITION FOR  THE NEWSPRINT  INDUSTRY As  Approved  on  November  17,  1933 BY PRESIDENT  ROOSEVELT Executive     Order An  application  having  been  duly  made,  pursuant  to  and  in  full compliance  with  the  provisions  of  Title  I  of  the  National  Industrial Recovery  Act,  approved  June  16,  1933,  for  my  approval  of  a  Code  of Fair  Competition  of  the  Newsprint  Industry,  and  hearings  having been  held  thereon  and  the  Administrator  having  rendered  his  report containing  an  analysis  of  the  said  Code  of  Fair  Competition  together with  his  recommendations  and  findings  with  respect  thereto,  and  the Administrator  having  found  that  tlie  said  Code  of  Fair  Competition complies  in  all  respects  with  the  pertinent  provisions  of  Title  I  of said  Act  and  that  the  requirements  of  clauses  (1)  and  (2)  of  subsec- tion (a)  of  Section  3  of  the  said  Act  have  been  met: NOW,  THEREFORE,  I,  Franklin  D.  Roosevelt,  President  of  the United  States,  pursuant  to  the  authority  vested  in  me  by  Title  I  of the  National  Industrial  Recovery  Act,  approved  June  16,  1933,  and otherwise,  do  adopt  and  approve  the  report,  recommendations,  and findings  of  the  Administrator  and  do  order  that  the  said  Code  of Fair  Competition  be  and  it  is  hereby  approved,  however,  feeling that  the  minimum  wage  for  this  industry  should  be  not  less  than forty  (40)  cents  per  hour,  my  order  of  approval  is  subject  to  the following  condition : That  within  90  days  from  the  effective  date  of  this  Code  the Administrator  hold  such  further  hearing  upon  such  notice  as  he, in  his  discretion,  shall  fix  for  the  purpose  of  determining  the  adequacy of  the  minimum  wages  established  in  said  Code,  after  which  his report  and  recommendation  shall  be  submitted  to  me  for  further  order which  order  shall  have  the  effect  of  a  condition  to  my  approval  of this  Code. WHEREAS after investigation I find 
and proclaim that there is an interrup­
tion of the operation of the Point Breeze 
plants and facilities of the Western Elec­
tric Company, Incorporated, in and ne*ar 
the City of Baltimore, Maryland, as a 
result of a Labor disturbance, that the 
war effort is being and will be unduly 
impeded or delayed by such interruption, 
and that the exercise of the power and 
authority vested in me is necessary to 
insure the operation of such plant in the 
interest of the war effort;
NOW, THEREFORE, by virtue of the 
power and authority vested in me by the 
Constitution and laws of the' United 
States, particularly the War Labor Dis­
putes Act (Public Law, 78th Cong.), as
^3 F.R. 2185.

8  8 F.R. 1911.
President of the United States and Com­
mander in Chief of the Army and Navy 
of the United States, it is hereby ordered 
and directed as follows:
The Secretary of War is authorized 
and directed to take immediate posses­
sion of and operate the Point Breeze 
plants and facilities of the Western Elec­
tric Company, Incorporated, in and near 
the City of Baltimore, Maryland, and to 
the extent that he deems necessary, is 
further authorized to take possession of 
and operate other installations in or near 
the City of Baltimore, Maryland, used or 
operated by said Company in connection 
with its operation of the foregoing plants 
and facilities. The Secretary of War is 
authorized and directed to do the fore­
going, through and with the aid of such 
persons or instrumentalities as he may 
designate, and insofar as may be neces­
sary or desirable, to produce the war ma­
terials called for by the Company’ s con­
tracts with the United States, its, depart­
ments and agencies or as may otherwise 
be required for the war effort, and do all 
things necessary or incidental to that 
end. The Secretary of War shall permit 
the management to continue with its 
managerial functions to the maximum 
degree possible consistent with the aims 
of this order.
The Secretary of War is authorized to 
take such action, if any, as he may deem 
necessary or desirable to provide protec­
tion for the plant and all persons em­
ployed or seeking employment therein.
In furtherance of the objectives set 
forth in Executive Order No. 9370.1  the 
Secretary of War is (1) authorized to 
request the National War Labor Board 
to consider the issuance of an order 
withholding or, withdrawing from the 
Point Breeze Employees Association any 
benefits, privileges or rights, accruing to 
the said Association under the terms or 
conditions of employment, in effect by 
agreement between the Company,and 
the Association or otherwise, until such 
time as the said Association has demon­
strated to the satisfaction of the Na­
tional War Labor Board its, willingness 
and capacity to comply with the terms 
and conditions of employment prescribed 
by the order of the National War Labor 
Board dated December 13, 1943; (2) di­
rected to recommend to the authorized 
federal agencies the entry of appropriate 
orders relating to the modification or 
cancellation of draft deferments or em­
ployment privileges, or both.
Possession and operation thereunder 
of the said plant and facilities shall be 
terminated by the Secretary of War 
within sixty days after he determines 
that the productive efficiency of the plant 
prevailing prior to the taking possession 
thereof has been restored.
F ranklin D R oosevelt

EXECUTIVE ORDER
Amending Certain P rovisions  op the 
Civil  S ervice R ules
By virtue of and pursuant to the au­
thority vested in me by the Civil Service 
Act (22 Stat. 403), and by section 1753 
of the Revised Statutes (U.S.C., title 5, 
sec. 631), the Civil Service Rules are 
hereby amended as follows:
Section 1 of Rule I is amended to 
read:
1. No interference with elections.  No 
person in the executive civil service shall 
use his official authority or influence for 
the purpose of interfering with an elec­
tion or affecting the results thereof. 
Persons who by the provisions of these 
rules are in the competitive classified 
service, while retaining the right to vote 
as they please and to express their opin­
ions on all political subjects, shall take 
no active part in political management 
or in political campaigns.
Section 5 of Rule X II is amended to 
read:
5. Retention of soldiers and sailors.  
In harmony with statutory provisions, 
when reductions are being made in the 
force, in any part of the classified serv­
ice, no employee entitled to military pref­
erence in appointment shall be dis­
charged, dropped, or reduced in rank or 
salary before any employee not entitled 
to military preference in competition 
with him if his record is good; nor shall 
any classified employee entitled to mili­
tary preference in appointment be dis­
charged, dropped, or reduced in rank or 
salary before any employee not entitled 
to military preference in competition 
with him if his efficiency rating is less 
than good but better than, or equal to, 
that of any such non-preference em­
ployee.
Civil Service Rule XV is amended to 
read:
Legal appointment necessary to com ­
pensation.  Whenever the Commission 
finds, after due notice and opportunity 
for explanation, that any person has been 
appointed to or is holding any position, 
whether by original appointment, pro­
motion, assignment, transfer, or rein­
statement, in violation of the Civil Serv­
ice Act or Rules, or of any Executive 
order or any regulation of the Commis­
sion, or that any employee subject 
thereto has violated such Act, Rules, 
orders, or regulations, it shall certify the 
facts to the proper appointing officer with 
specific instructions as to discipline or 
dismissal of the person or employee af­
fected. If the appointing officer fails 
to carry out the instructions of the Com­
mission within 10 days after receipt 
thereof, the Commission shall certify 
the facts to the proper disbursing and 
auditing officers, and such officers shall 
make no payment or allowance of the 
salary or wages of any such person or 
employee thereafter accruing.
This order shall be effective as of 
November 7, 1940.
F ranklin D R oosevelt
T he W hite  H ouse,
March 5,1941.

Executive Order

MOobDIFYING THE CopDE OF Farr COMPETITION FOR THE BAKING INDUSTRY
AND THE ORDER OF APPROVAL THEREOF

ORDER NO. 445-2

WHEREAS, certain facts have heen submitted by members of the Baking
Industry indicating the necessity of certain modifications in the Code of Fair Competi-
tion for said Industry, as approved by me on May 28, 1934; and

WHEREAS, it appears necessary in the public interest to make such modifica-
tions in order to effectuate the purposes of the Act;

NOW, THEREFORE, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States,
pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery
Act, upon due consideration of the facts and upon the recommendation of the Adminis-
trator for Industrial Recovery, hereby order:

1. That the effective date of the Code of Fair Competition for the Baking Indus-
try be and the same hereby is stayed until July 9, 1934;

2. That the second condition of the Order of May 28, 1934, approving the said
code, staying the provisions of Article VII, Section 6, until my further order, is hereby
eliminated and the provisions of said section shall be in full force and effect on the
effective date of said code.

3. That the period within which the Code Authority is to report its investiga-
tion of the operation and the effect of the provisions of Articles III, IV, and V to me
is hereby extended from the date designated in said order of approval to November

15, 1934.
FRANKLIN D ROOSEVELT

United States Grain Standards Act, 1916

to the official grain standards of the

that they shall be published now. There­
fore, It is hereby ordered,  That the text

Regulations be amended as follows:
1. In § 26.101 Strick out the definition 
of wheat found in the second paragraph 
and insert in lieu thereof:
Wheat. Wheat shall be any grain 
which, before the removal of dockage, 
consists of 50 percent or more of wheat 
and not more than 10 percent of other 
grains for which standards have been 
established under the provisions of the 
United States Grain Standards Act, and 
which, after the removal of dockage, con­
tains not more than 50 percent of broken 
kernels of grain of any size. The term 
wheat in these standards shall not in­
clude emmer, spelt, einkom, Polish 
wheat, and poulard wheat.
2. In § 26.103 add a footnote reference
(2) at Grade No. 4 as follows:
• Wheat of this class that contains more  
than 10 percent of broken kernels of grain  
that will pass through a 20-gage metal sieve  
with slotted perforations 0.064 inch Wide  
by % inch long shall not be graded higher  
than No. 4. •  „
3. In §§ 26.108, 26.110, and 26.112 add 
a footnote reference (1) at Grade No. 4 
as follows:
1 Wheat of this class that contains •  more  
than 10 percent of broken kernels of grain  
that will pass through a 20-gage metal sieve  
with slotted perforations 0.064 inch wide  
by % inch long shall not be graded higher  
than No. 4.
4. In § 26.106 add footnote reference
(3) at Grade No. 4 as follows:
5 * Wheat of each of these classes that con­
tains more than 15 percent of broken ker­
nels of grain of any size shall not be graded  
higher than No. 4.
5. In §§ 26.103, 26.106, 26.108, 26.110, 
and 26.112 strike out words “or more than 
10 percent of cracked kernels” from the 
specifications for Sample grade in each 
of the tables of grade requirements.

26.308, 26.358, 26.409, 26.504 and 26.563 
paragraph (c) of each of these sections 
is amended to read as follows:
(c) Percentage of moisture.  Percent­
age of moisture shall be that ascertained 
by the air oven and the method of use 
thereof described in Service and Regu­
latory Announcements No. 147 of the 
Bureau of Agricultural Economics of the 
United States Department of Agricul­
ture, or ascertained by any device and 
method which give equivalent results in 
the determination of moisture.
7. In §  26.461 amend paragraph (c) to 
read as follows:
(c) Percentage of moisture.  Percent­
age of moisture shall be that ascertained 
by the apparatus and thè method of use 
thereof specified in the official grain 
standards of the United States for the 
kind of grain which predominates in the 
mixture.
8. In § 26.121 paragraph (i) is deleted.
9. In § 26.155 strike out the words 
“ (corn and other grains)” under the 
heading “Damaged kernels”.

the words “ and other grains.”

“Foreign material” insert 3 in lieU of 2

and insert in lieu thereof:
“ Cereal oats” shall be any oats, 
whether sized, clipped, or natural, which 
contain more than 20 percent of oats 
and/or other matter except “Fine seeds” 
that will pass through a 20-gage metal 
sieve with slotted perforation 0.064 
inch wide by % inch long.
13. In § 26.260 strike out definition and 
insert in lieu thereof :
“Smutty oats” shall be oats which have 
the kernels covered with smut spores, Or 
which contain smut masses and/or smut 
balls in excess of 0.2 percent.

(i) Fine seeds.  Fine seeds shall in­
clude all matter which can be removed 
from oats by the use of a metal sieve per­
fec te d  with equilateral triangular per­
forations the inscribed circles of which

2. Schedule of fees payable to wit­
nesses, foreign counsel, and interpreters.
(a) Witnesses. Each witness whose 
testimony is obtained under a commis­
sion to take testimony in connection 
with foreign documents for use in crimi-
nal cases shall be entitled to receive 
compensation at the rate of $5 a day 
for each day of attendance, plus 5 
cents a mile for going from his place of 
residence or business to the place of 
examination and returning, by the 
shortest feasible route. When, however, 
it is necessary to procure the attend­
ance of a witness on behalf of the 
United States or an indigent party, an 
officer or agent of the United States 
may negotiate with the witness to pay 
compensation at such higher rate as 
may be approved by the Attorney Gen­
eral, plus the mileage allowance stated 
above. The compensation and mileage 
of each witness shall be paid by the 
party, or parties, applying for the com­
mission, -unless the commission is ac­
companied by an order of court that all 
fees, compensation, and other expenses 
authorized by these regulations are 
chargeable to the United States under 
section 7 of the said act of June 20, 
1936 (28 U.S.C. Supp. sec. 695f (b)).
(b) Counsel. Each counsel who rep­
resents a party to the action or proceed­
ing in the examination before the com­
missioner shall receive compensation for 
each day of attendance at a rate of 
not less than $5 a day and not more 
than $25 a day, as agreed between him 
and the party whom he represents, plus 
such actual and necessary expenses as 
may be allowed by the commissioner 
upon verified statements filed with him. 
If the commission is issued on applica­
tion of the United States, the compen­
sation and expense of counsel represent­
ing each party are chargeable to the 
United States. If the commission is is­
sued on application of any other party, 
the compensation and expense of coun­
sel shall be paid by the party whom such 
counsel represents, unless the commis­
sion is accompanied by an order of court 
that all fees, compensation, and other 
expenses authorized by these regulations 
are chargeable to the United States un­
der section 7 of the said act of June 20 
1936 (28 U.S.C. Supp. sec. 695f (b)).
(c) Interpreters and translators.  Each 
interpreter and translator employed by 
the commissioner under these regula­
tions shall receive an allowance of $5 
a day, plus 5 cents a mile for going from, 
his place of residence or business to the 
place of examination and returning, by 
the shortest feasible route. The com­
pensation and mileage of interpreters 
and translators shall be chargeable to 
the United States.

foregoing regulations, by the commis­
sioner at the conclusion of their serv­
ices. Other expenses authorized by 
these regulations shall be paid by the 
commissioner as they are incurred.

By virtue of the authority vested in me 
by the Constitution and statutes, as Pres­
ident of the United States, and in order 
to meet the manpower requirements of 
our armed forces and our expanding war 
production program by a fuller utiliza­
tion of our available manpower, it is 
hereby ordered:
J. For the duration of the war, no 
plant, factory or other place of employ­
ment shall be deemed to be making the 
most effective utilization of its manpower 
if the minimum workweek therein is less 
than 48 hours per week.
2. All departments and agencies of the 
Federal Government shall require their 
contractors to comply with the minimum 
workweek prescribed in this order and 
with policies, directives, and regulations 
prescribed hereunder, and shall prompt­
ly take such action as may be necessary 
for that purpose.
3. The Chairman of the War Man-/ 
power Commission shall determine all 
questions of interpretation and applica­
tion arising under this order and shall 
formulate and ilssue such policies, direc­
tives, and regulations as he determines to 
be necessary to carry out this order and 
to effectuate its purposes. r Çhe Chair­
man of the War Manpower Commission 
is authorized to establish a m inim um 
workweek greater or less than that estab­
lished in section 1  of This order or take 
other action with respect to any case or 
type of case in which he determines that 
such different minimum workweek or 
other action would more effectively con­
tribute to the war effort and promote the 
purposes of this order.
4. All departments and agencies of the 
Federal Government shall comply with 
such policies, directives, and regulations 
as the Chairman of the War Manpower 
Commission sliall prescribe pursuant to 
this order, and shall so utilize their facil­
ities, services, and personnel, and take 
such action under authority vested in 
them by law, as the Chairman deter­
mines to be necessary to effectuate the
purposes of this order and promote com­
pliance with its provisions.
5. Nothing in this order shall be con­
strued as superseding or in conflict with 
any Federal, State or local law limiting 
hours of work or with the provisions of 
any individual or collective bargaining 
agreement with respect to rates of pay 
for hours worked in excess of the agreed 
or customary workweek, nor shall this 
order be construed as suspending or 
modifying any provision of the Fair La­
bor Standards Act (Act of June 25,1938; 
52 Stat. 1060; 29 U.S.C. 201 et seq.) or 
any other Federal, State or local law re­
lating to the payment of wages or over­
time.

EXECUTIVE ORDER 9332
Establishing the S olid F uels A dminis ­
tration for War
By virtue of the authority vested in 
me by the Constitution and statutes of 
the United States, as President of the 
United States and Commander in Chief 
of the Army and Navy, it is hereby or­
dered as follows:
1. Whenever used in this Order:
<a) The term “solid fuels” includes all 
forms of anthracite, bituminous, sub- 
bituminous, and lignitic coals (including 
packaged and processed fuels, such as 
briquettes).
(b) The term “solid fuels industries” 
means the development, production, 
preparation, treatment, processing, stor­
age, shipment, receipt, and distribution of 
solid fuels within the United States, its 
territories and possessions, but does not 
include the transportation of solid fuels. \j
(c) The term “transportation” means 
transportation as defined in the Inter­
state Commerce Act, as amended, and in 
Executive Orders Nos. 8989 and 9156.
(d) The terms “distribution” and 
“shipment” exclude transportation, and 
the terms “distribute” and “ship” exclude 
transport.
(e) The term “directive” includes or­
der, regulation, and any other similar 
instrument.
2. There is established within the De­
partment of the Interior a Solid Fuels 
Administration for War, at the head of 
which shall be a Solid Fuels Administra­
tor, hereinafter referred to as the Ad­
ministrator. The Secretary of the In ­
terior shall serve ex-officio as Adminis­trator.
3. The Administrator shall:
(a) Subject to the provisions of this 
Order, establish basic policies and formu­
late plans and programs to assure for the 
prosecution of the war the conservation 
and most effective development and uti­
lization of solid fuels in the United States 
and its territories and possessions, issue 
necessary policy and operating directives 
to partieaengaged in the solid fuels in­
dustries, and appoint such general, re­
gional, local, or functional solid fuels 
industries committees or councils as the
Administrator finds necessary, Provided 
that no directive issued hereunder shall 
conflict with any directive which has 
heretofore been issued or may hereafter 
be issued (1) by the Chairman of the 
War Production Board pursuant to para­
graph one of Executive Order No. 9125 
of April 7, 1942, or <2) by the Chairman 
of the War Manpower Commission pur­
suant to Executive Orders Nos. 9139 of 
April 18, 1942, 9279 of December 5, 1942, 
and 9301 of February 9, 1943.
<b) Serve, as far as practicable, as the 
liaison and channel of communication 
between parties engaged in the sold fuels 
industries and the several departments 
and agencies of the Federal Government 
on matters directly involving the func­
tions of the Administrator.
(c) Obtain from the Departments of 
War and the Navy, the several divisions 
and branches of the War Production 
Board, such other Federal and state de­
partments and agencies as may be ap­
propriate, and from any other sources, 
private or governmental, any informa­
tion, statistics, and data necessary to 
effectuate the purposes of this Order.
(d) (1) Prepare estimates as to the 
quantities of solid fuels which the Ad­
ministrator deems necessary to meet di­
rect and indirect military, and essential 
industrial and civilian requirements and 
submit such estimates with recommenda­
tions to the War Production Board.
(2) Recommend to the War Produc­
tion Board any program for distribution 
of solid fuels which the Administrator 
deems necessary to meet direct and in­
direct military, and essential industrial 
requirements.
<3) Prepare and submit to the War 
Production Board recommendations as to 
the kinds and quantities of materials 
needed by parties engaged in the solid 
fuels industries to make available solid 
fuels in such quantities as the Adminis­
trator deems necessary to meet direct and 
indirect military, and essential industrial 
and civilian requirements.
(e) Subject to the direction of the 
Chairman of the War Production Board, 
exercise the powers, authority, and the 
discretion conferred upon the Chairman 
by Paragraph 1  of Executive Order No. 
9125 of April 7, 1942, by issuing, and tak­
ing appropriate action to enforce, such

4. In the performance of his func­
tions, the Administrator shall consult 
with the appropriate authorities in the

and agencies shall supply such infor­

may require-in performing his functions 
and shall advise with the Administrator 
before undertaking any action which 
might affect the continuous, ready avail­
ability of solid fuels for direct and in­

assist him in carrying out the purposes 
of this Order, the Administrator may es­
tablish committees or designate groups

partments or agencies of the Federal

termine, any and all power, authority, 
and discretion conferred upon him by 
this Order. The Administrator may 
designate either the Deputy Adminis­
trator or the Acting Secretary of the In­
terior to serve as Acting Solid Fuels 
Administrator in the absence of the Ad­
ministrator. The Administrator and 
Deputy Administrator may (a) exercise 
the powers, authority, and discretion 
conferred upon them by or under the 
provisions of this Order through such 
personnel of the Solid Fuels Adminis­
tration for War and the Department of 
the Interior, and in such manner as the 
Administrator or Deputy Administrator 
may determine, and (b) accept the serv­
ices of other departments, agencies, and 
officials of the Government In carrying 
out the purposes of this Order. The Ad­
ministrator, within the limits of such 
funds as may be allocated or appropri­
ated for the purpose, may employ neces­
sary personnel and make provision for 
necessary supplies, facilities, travel and 
services.
7. In the performance of his functions 
the Administrator shall, to the fullest 
extent compatible with efficiency, utilize 
appropriate existing agencies, facilities 
and services of the Department of the 
Interior.
8. The Office of Solid Fuels Coordina­
tion for National Defense established 
pursuant to letter of the President dated 
November 5, 1 9 ,4 1  (changed to the Office 
of Solid Fuels Coordinator for War by 
letter of the President dated May 25, 
1942) is abolished, and its personnel, 
records, property, and funds are trans­
ferred to the Solid Fuels Administration
for War, effective fifteen days from the 
date of this Order. All directives, 
agreements, recommendations, and 
other documents issued or entered into 
under the functions, duties, and author­
ities of the Solid Fuels Coordinator for 
War shall remain in force as the re­
sponsibility of the Administrator until 
such time as he may revoke, alter, or 
Otherwise change such documents under 
provisions of this Executive order.
9. The Administrator shall keep the 
President informed with respect to the 
progress made in carrying out this Order 
and perform such related duties as the 
President may from time to time assign

deemed to limit in any way the statutory

An application having been duly made, pursuant to and in full compliance with
the provisions of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16,
1933, for my approval of a Code of Fair Competition for the Medium and Low Priced
Jewelry Manufacturing Industry, and hearings having been held thereon and the
Administrator having rendered his report containing an analysis of the said Code of
Fair Competition together with his recommendations and findings with respect
thereto, and the Administrator having found that the said Code of Fair Competition
complies in all respects with the pertinent provisions of Title I of said Act and that
the requirements of clauses (1) and (2) of subsection (a) of Section 3 of the said Act
have been met:

NOW, THEREFORE, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States,
pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery
Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do adopt and approve the report, recom-
mendations and findings of the Administrator and do order that the said Code of
Fair Competition be and is hereby approved, subject to the following condition:

That the application of the provision of sub-section (b), Section 1, Article III,
which provides for the payment of time and one third for all hours worked by any
employee in excess of forty (40) per week, shall be stayed until March 1, 1934, at
which time such provision shall become effective and have the same force and effect
as any other provision of the Code.

FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT.

Approval Recommended:

Administrator.

356 That  the  application  of  the  provision  of  sub-section  (b) ,  Section  1, Article  III,  which  provides  for  the  payment  of  time  and  one  third for  all  hours  worked  by  any  employee  in  excess  of  forty  (40)  per week,  shall  be  stayed  until  March  1,  1934,  at  which  time  such  provi- sion shall  become  effective  and  have  the  same  force  and  effect  as  any other  provision  of  the  Code.

Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved Code of Fair Competition of the Paper and Pulp Industry before June 14, 1935 are accrued consequences that the repeal did not turn into continuing commands; nothing in S.J. Res. 113 (SUPPLEMENT:SJRES113) continues the approval after June 14, 1935. Any antitrust exemption for complying action before the repeal (NIRA section 5, SUPPLEMENT:NIRA5) is likewise an accrued effect; the resolution's proviso, which extends the exemption only to "agreements and action thereunder" meeting stated conditions, leaves open how far it narrowed the exemption for past action, so the claim records no continuing exemption and no surviving approval. Any hearing held, report made or further order issued under the condition before the repeal is an accrued act, not a continuing command.

A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935: the Court held the section 3 code-making delegation unconstitutional and the Live Poultry Code provisions in question invalid. Recorded as a validity characterization for every section 3 code approval, not as this order's end; the judgment did not cancel or withdraw this order.

NIRA section 3 (48 Stat. 195, June 16, 1933): under 3(a) the President approved codes and could impose conditions of approval; under 3(b), 3(c) and 3(f) an approved code's provisions became standards of fair competition enforceable by injunction and as misdemeanors. These are the legal effects that section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed.

NIRA section 5 exempted from the antitrust laws any code approved and in effect under Title I and any complying action while Title I was in effect and for sixty days thereafter; any exemption for action taken before the repeal is an accrued effect, not continued operation of the approval.

IV NRA Codes 355. (Dec 23, 1933)'. Quotations are taken from the registered file, not from the unregistered clause-drafts copy. EO 6530 (December 23, 1933) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Medium and Low Priced Jewelry Manufacturing Industry 'subject to the following condition: That the application of the provision of sub-section (b), Section 1, Article III, which provides for the payment of time and one third for all hours worked by any employee in excess of forty (40) per week, shall be stayed until March 1, 1934, at which time such provision shall become effective and have the same force and effect as any other provision of the Code.' The dossier's single clause (characters 757-1620) holds two commands with different lifetimes, so the inventory is corrected on the registered text into two scopes: the approval sentence (757-1158) and the stay condition (1160-1525); the signature block and Administrator's recommendation that follow are not operative. Stay condition: it ends by its own terms on 1934-03-01, recorded inclusive (the stay runs through that day) under the owner's 2026-10-21 ruling; the words 'at which time such provision shall become effective' support the exclusive reading, under which the stay stops when March 1, 1934 begins and the overtime provision applies that day. The dossier's own-terms record (until_event, 1934-03-01) matches. After the stay the overtime provision is a provision of the code, not a command of this order. No held order extends, shortens or revokes the stay (searches below; the type rule's outlier case of a stay later modified by administrative order cannot be excluded beyond the held sources). Approval: First end: 1935-06-14, the day Senate Joint Resolution 113 (Public Resolution No. 26, 74th Congress, 49 Stat. 375, chapter 246) was approved. Section 2 of the resolution reads: 'All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed', with one proviso that narrows only the section 5 antitrust exemption. It names no code and no order, so it is not a naming instrument (owner ruling 2026-10-21, unnamed instruments), and under the owner's 2026-10-28 ruling a general rule ends a command only where something shows it extinguished that command. What shows it here is the text of the Act under which the order was made (48 Stat. 195, held): section 3(a) is the power to approve a code; section 3(b) makes the provisions of an approved code 'the standards of fair competition for such trade or industry' and a violation an unfair method of competition; section 3(c) gives the district courts jurisdiction to restrain violations of 'any code of fair competition approved under this title'; and section 10(b) lets the President cancel or modify 'any order, approval, license, rule, or regulation issued under this title', which shows the approval was a continuing act that the Act made binding through sections 3(b) and 3(c). The approval commands nothing of its own beyond that statutory operation, and the resolution repealed the approval power and the enforcement of codes together, with no clause preserving approved codes. The order's only operative act, making the code the enforceable standard, therefore ended on 1935-06-14. Alternatives considered and disclosed. (a) Earlier: Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U.S. 495, decided May 27, 1935 (caption and syllabus held), says at 542 'the code-making authority thus conferred is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power'. The judgment concerned the Live Poultry Code; it names no other code, and nothing held shows it extinguished this approval on that date (no order of May 27 through June 14 touches any code). If a reviewer holds it ended every approval, the first end would be 1935-05-27; the claim uses June 14 because that is the first date on which held text removes approval and enforcement for all codes. (b) The original expiry of Title I two years after enactment (section 2(c), June 16, 1935) was displaced when the resolution amended section 2(c) to April 1, 1936; it is later than the repeal. (c) Later: EO 7076 (June 15, 1935, held APP text, page record date 1935-06-15; its held transcription omits the signature and date lines) amends all existing Title I executive orders 'so as to continue them in effect and to extend their operation ... until April 1, 1936, so far as consistent with the provisions of the National Industrial Recovery Act as amended and extended', but provides that it 'shall not be construed as an exercise by the President of any authority, or as authorizing any person or agency ... to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition, to provide for the enforcement of such codes'. Because the approval's force came through the provisions the resolution had repealed the day before, continuing it 'so far as consistent' with the Act as amended leaves it no enforceable operation; EO 7076 is therefore recorded here as a disclosed later order and is not treated as an extension or an end. Held EO 7075 (June 15, 1935) likewise refers to the trades 'heretofore subject to codes of fair competition'. (d) A reviewer who reads section 5 as keeping approved codes 'in effect' for antitrust exemption while Title I stood (to April 1, 1936, plus sixty days) could place a later end for that statutory exemption; the exemption is a statutory consequence, not a command of this order, and the resolution's proviso narrowed it to agreements on section 7(a) requirements and on practices already unlawful. That reading would not revive the approval as an enforceable code. Limit: the approved code's own text is not held, so a duration or cancellation term inside it could not be read; no held order, statute, case or index entry shows a code-specific cancellation, amendment, supersession or expiry. The order states no savings. What survives the repeal is statutory and accrued, not a continuing command of the approval: liabilities and rights that accrued while the code was binding (violations before 1935-06-14, and conduct that complied with it), and the section 5 antitrust exemption for action complying with an approved code 'while this title is in effect ... and for sixty days thereafter' (held, 48 Stat. 195), as narrowed by the resolution's proviso. None of these keeps the approval operative after 1935-06-14. Whether pre-repeal violations remained prosecutable turns on a general saving rule that is not held and is not relied on. For the stay, the overtime provision that took effect on 1934-03-01 is a provision of the code, which ended with the approval's enforceable operation; it is not a surviving command of this order.

The WPA list dates the order June 15, 1934; the page heading, the census register and the held text all say June 16, 1934. The one-day difference does not change identity (number, subject and the NRA Codes citation agree) and enters no end date below, because every end is keyed to the order's own stated July 9, 1934 or to the June 14, 1935 repeal. The order has three numbered operative clauses, which I have read separately: (1) 'the effective date of the Code of Fair Competition for the Baking Industry be and the same hereby is stayed until July 9, 1934'; (2) the second condition of the approving order, which stayed a provision of article VII 'until my further order', 'is hereby eliminated and the provisions of said section shall be ... in full force and effect on the effective date of said code' (the held text reads 'Section G'; the approving order of May 28, 1934, held as a separate APP text, states the stayed provision as 'Section 6', so 'G' is evidently a transcription error for '6'; the lifecycle does not depend on which section); (3) the period in which the Code Authority is to report on the operation and effect of articles III, IV and V 'is hereby extended from the date designated in said order of approval to November 15, 1934'. The machine inventory (three clauses, characters 654 to 789, 791 to 1074 and 1076 to 1426) is complete and correct; the lead-in recital, the 'ORDER NO. 445-2' heading and the signature block command nothing, so no replacement inventory is needed. The dossier's own-terms leads are right for clause 1 (a stated date, July 9, 1934) and clause 3 (a report deadline), and wording matches only for clause 2 ('until my further order' describes the stay that clause 2 removes; clause 2 itself states no period).

Clause 1: once the stay ran through July 9, 1934 the code's effective date arrived and the code took effect; that is a completed effect of the stay and keeps nothing of the stay operative. Clauses 2 and 3: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the code before June 14, 1935 are completed (accrued) effects of the approval; the general savings statute of the time, which ordinarily preserves liabilities incurred under a repealed statute, is not a held source, and the repeal text contains no savings clause. Section 5 of title I exempted from the antitrust laws any code approved and in effect under the title and any action complying with it taken during the period; the resolution's proviso limits that exemption to agreements and action thereunder of two stated kinds and states no time limit, so the held text does not settle whether it narrowed the exemption for action taken under codes before June 14, 1935. Whatever exemption or liability survives for past action is an accrued effect of completed acts, not continued operation of this approval. No held source shows a prosecution, injunction or other proceeding under this code continuing after June 14, 1935, and nothing continues the approval itself.

EO 9301 (February 9, 1943, Franklin D. Roosevelt; 8 FR 1825, issue of Thursday, February 11, 1943), read in full in the held Federal Register text, declares that "For the duration of the war" no plant or place of employment is deemed to make the most effective use of manpower if its minimum workweek is under 48 hours (section 1, inside the lead row of the machine inventory), directs agencies to require contractors to comply (2), authorizes the Chairman of the War Manpower Commission to interpret the order and issue policies, directives and regulations and to set a different workweek in particular cases (3), requires agencies to comply (4) and states that the order is not to supersede other hours or wage laws (5). The phrase "For the duration of the war" is an own-terms condition; no held instrument or source fixes a legal end of the war before August 30, 1945, and EO 9607 revokes the order outright without reciting that it had lapsed, so the first end is the express revocation.

EO 10697 contains no savings or transition clause. It prescribes a complete new Tariff of Fees and its own collection rules (sections 1-6), effective March 1, 1957, and revokes the earlier tariff orders to the extent not already revoked or superseded. Fees charged under the earlier tariff were completed transactions; the order created no fund, office, property or vested right that survived.
